The fit's t0 is not what we thought — a trigger prior, and the sharing mechanisms, measured

2026-08-12 · det3 saturday run (490 V / 1000 V) · working through the reconstruction handoff (T1.1, T1.2, T1.5) · records in mx_june_wft/T0_PRIOR_2026-08-11.md and mx_june_wft/SHARING_DEPTH_2026-08-11.md

TL;DR. (1) The forward fit's t0 carries far less information than assumed: production values are grid-locked, the χ² surface has a one-depth-bin (60 ns) tooth ambiguity with only ~34% of planes in the physical tooth, and the reported t0_err (~1.5 ns) is fiction. (2) The scintillator trigger + ftst predict t0 per event to ~4 ns; a Gaussian prior on that prediction is implemented, calibrated, and validated out-of-sample: within5 +0.44%, reco_far −0.44%, core σ −4.6%, implied-v flatness better on both planes, 14% faster, nothing regresses. Recommended for adoption on det3. (3) A model-free measurement separates the X/Y sharing mechanisms: Y's neighbours keep discharging after the drift column ends (RC transport), X's fall with the central strip — but X's copy is also delayed, so F6's strong form ("X cannot share resistively") needs softening. (4) Two traps found: the 2026-08-06 merge silently dropped part of the validated production model (kTauY) — and the naive restoration regressed Y badly (σY 1.14 → 1.57°), the F19 representation-dependence lesson again, so the per-plane τ goes back in through recalibration instead; and dt_xy exists in three inconsistent generations.

1 · What the fitted t0 actually is (the T1.1 gate)

The handoff item asked a simple question: the DREAM trigger is a scintillator-pair coincidence (~5 ns) and ftst records its phase against the 60 ns sampling clock — so the fit's t0 is predictable per event, and today it is fitted freely. Is the prediction worth using? The gate measurement (spread of fitted t0 within one ftst class vs the fit's own uncertainty) answered a different, bigger question: what the fit's t0 actually is.

findingsizeevidence
production t0 is grid-locked59% (X) / 80% (Y) values sit exactly on a 10 ns lattice — the coarse scan's 5 ns snap; Nelder-Mead never moved t0
one-depth-bin tooth ambiguityonly ~34% in the physical tooth pooled (t0 + 10·ftst) shows teeth at exactly 60 ns spacing; q_uend medians 780/720/660 ns across teeth −1/0/+1 — the whole fitted column slides one bin. The central tooth's 720 ns matches det3's real column span, so the mode is the physical solution
drag along the p0–t0 valley±60–100 ns χ²(t0) at reference-pinned geometry: one sharp minimum per event whose location scatters; a free refit moved t0 by >30 ns for 53–58% of events
t0_err is fictitious~1.5 ns reported it is the fixed-(p0,w) curvature; the soft direction is the valley (δp0 = w·δt0) — the F25 caveat, now measured

Why this matters for geometry: a 60 ns tooth error moves p0 by w·60 ns ≈ 0.3–0.9 mm on inclined tracks — larger than the 0.33 mm floor. The handoff's expectation that the prior "will not move position" assumed δt0 ≈ 5 ns; the real ambiguity is 60 ns.

2 · The prior: calibration and A/B

The prediction table t0_pred(plane, ftst) is calibrated from ref-pinned fits on the 7,093 bench-cache events (class medians, SE ≈ 4 ns) — and the −10 ns/step ftst ladder emerges cleanly from the data, which is the direct validation that ftst → t0 prediction works. Implementation: a Gaussian penalty in chi2_plane(..., t0_prior=(t0_pred, σ)), bundle fields t0_abs / t0_prior_sigma, per-plane ftst plumbed through the driver and written to the event table. The prior also collapses the global scan's t0 axis (7 points → 1), which pays for the §21.1 p0-window widening later.

A/B on the even half (σ ∈ {25, 10, 5}), winner validated on the held-out odd half:

odd half, n = 3,546within5reco_farcore σ [mm] med |r| [mm]σθ X/Y [°]implied-v spread X/Ys/fit
baseline93.27%2.66%0.4820.743 1.17 / 1.111.1 / 1.11.08
σ = 5 ns prior93.71%2.22%0.460 0.7141.15 / 1.100.8 / 0.80.93

Nothing regresses; the winner is cleaner out-of-sample than in the scan. Mechanism check (tooth population): even at σ = 5 only ~33% of fits land within 30 ns of the prediction — the model's per-event χ² preference for a displaced t0 beats a 144-unit penalty. The gains come from starting the fit at the physical t0 and tipping near-degenerate basins, not from forcing the time base. What caps the prior is the model's own time drag — worst on Y. That is the quantitative bridge to the kernel work below: fix the Y kernel, then the prior can be meaningfully tight. Recommendation: adopt on det3 (t0_abs + σ = 5 in the bundle); fleet rollout needs the per-run calibration (08_t0_abs_calib.py); re-tune after the kernel merge.

3 · X/Y sharing mechanisms, measured without a model (T1.2 first leg)

The simulation's claim (F6): the ESL resistive strips run along y, so Y gets genuine resistive (RC) sharing and X cannot — X's ±1 sharing must be drift diffusion. The mechanisms differ in time, and the difference needs no model where it is sharpest: after the drift column ends, an RC-shared neighbour keeps discharging; a diffusion-shared neighbour must fall with the central strip.

observable (centered)XYreading
±1 peak / central0.380.42comparable at ±1
±1 peak delay~+70 ns~+90 nsboth dispersed — X is not purely prompt
±2 peak / central0.060.15the mechanism split: cascaded transport is Y's
past the column end→ 0stays positivethe RC signature, nearly absent on X
central undershoot−2%−10%independently reproduces the T14 "detector-side Y undershoot"

So the asymmetry is real and has the predicted sign — but the strong form of F6 is too strong: X has a weak, slow sharing channel too (inter-strip capacitance, groove leakage, or readout). A depth-dependent X kernel should replace part of X's discrete sharing, not all of it. The model hook (cX, an X-only scale on the discrete kernel) is in place; the refit arm (cX = 0, σp0/Dp refit) is queued.

4 · Two traps that affect everything else

The 2026-08-06 merge silently dropped part of the validated production model. The bench harness's variant switches (MODEL_FRAC, PRESCAN_COARSE, ROBUST_REFIT, SCORE_MODE, ITER_SCAN) lived in the RC-ladder line; the merge kept the other line and archived them, so the harness has been setting switches that nothing reads. Worse, production ran with kTauY = 1.78 (the measured τX 230 / τY 410 ns per-plane time constant) — the shipped bundles still carry the value, the shipped model never read it. The reference events.parquet is not reproducible by the shipped code. The naive restoration was A/B-tested and rejected: switching kTauY = 1.78 on under the shipped kernel form regressed Y badly (σY 1.14 → 1.57°, implied-v spread 1.0 → 5.0, core σ 0.437 → 0.461 mm) — lp2's hypers are self-consistent without it in this representation, exactly the F19 / beam-transplant lesson (RC constants are representation-dependent). The per-plane τ hook is kept under a new key (tau_y_fac) that no existing bundle carries, so nothing changes silently, and the constant will be re-fit under the shipped kernel instead of ported.

dt_xy has three inconsistent generations: −18.8 ns (the R&D fallback still hard-coded in reco.py/model.py), −7.65/−16.01 ns (the reference document), and +5.4/+30.2 ns (the shipped det3 bundle). t0's registration depends on the kernel form, so dt_xy is bundle-specific — this must be sorted before anyone enables select_pair or fit_joint. Keying by ftst difference is itself approximate: the calibrated table gives dt for diff = +1 ranging −7.8 to −18.8 ns depending on which (ftstx, ftsty) pair realises it.

5 · Housekeeping done alongside

  • t0_err added to the fit output (three-parameter curvature), per-plane ftst and an isochronous flag (F32's one-liner) now written to the event table.
  • Reference-document corrections: drift gap ~29 → 30.000 mm (the Al frame is the spacer), K = 18 noted as det3-specific (fleet refit at K = 22), §20's "never fix t0 from an external clock" superseded, §22 marked "fit_joint not in the executed path", §14.3 pointed at the archived per-plane kernel.

6 · The kernel arms — three informative negatives

  • The shipped chain has been running with kY ~47% too strong. Refitting (tau_y_fac, kY) under the shipped kernel from lp2's exact values dropped ref-pinned χ² by 23%, landing at tau_y_fac = 1.13 and kY = 1.96 (lp2 carries 2.88, optimal only under the archived RC-ladder kernel). On the bench this arm is a trade: it halves the long-documented Y angle-compression bias at |tan| > 0.14 (cmp14 −0.27 → −0.11) and runs 34% faster, but near-vertical Y worsens — so the per-plane τ goes in through a full recalibration, not a 2-parameter refit.
  • cX = 0 (diffusion-only X) is disfavoured: X's implied-v spread degrades 1.0 → 1.5 and an X angle bias appears. The discrete X copy carries real geometric information — consistent with §3's measured +70 ns X copy delay. T1.2 is answered: X's sharing is not diffusion booked twice.
  • The §21.1 shear (evaluate the scan at p0 − w·umid) is rejected as implemented — slightly worse everywhere. (The first explanation written here — "the amp-weighted centroid already sits near the mesh, so the lever overshoots" — was falsified the next morning by measuring the lever; see §7.)
  • Both refits' 23% χ² gains produced no geometry gain — §35's v↔kernel valley warning, verbatim. Implied-v flatness stays the only trustworthy judge.

Net adoptable result of the day: the σ = 5 trigger prior (§2). Records: KERNEL_ARMS_2026-08-12.md, T0_PRIOR_2026-08-11.md, SHARING_DEPTH_2026-08-11.md.

7 · Follow-through (2026-08-12): every arm judged, two items closed for real

7.1 · The prior is production-packaged

calib_bundle_lp2_t0p = lp2 + t0_abs + t0_prior_sigma = 5. A 400-event smoke run through the bare bundle (no CLI flags) reproduces the flag-driven run metric-for-metric — the prior activates from the bundle fields alone. This is the recommended det3 production configuration.

7.2 · T2.4 closed — and the first explanation was wrong

Measuring the scan lever from reference tracks (ueff = (pc − p0ref)/w on inclined events) gives +391 ns (X) / +377 ns (Y), angle-independent — i.e. the umid = 410 ns the rejected arm assumed was essentially correct, killing the "centroid sits near the mesh" explanation in §6. The real mechanism: p0 − w·ueff is exactly the level-set the χ² constrains best (the charge centroid), so a sheared scan grid lies along the p0–w valley and loses its w discrimination. A half-lever arm (200 ns) confirmed it: degradation is monotonic in shear strength. Any future §21.1 fix must score w along the sheared line with something other than the raw χ² minimum.

7.3 · T2.1 closed as far as recalibration can take it

A full 8-parameter recalibration (all hypers + tau_y_fac, v pinned) found a second equal-χ² basin: kY back at lp2's 2.90 with tau_y_fac = 1.39 and a faster shared τ (145 → 116 ns) — against the 2-parameter refit's kY 1.96 / fac 1.13. Two lessons and a verdict:

  • The C1_MIN floor is needed even with v pinned — an unguarded first run slid straight into the det7 collapse valley (c1 0.028, kY 3.9).
  • On the bench, both basins are the same trade: the deep-angle Y compression genuinely improves (cmp14 −0.27 → −0.18), near-vertical Y genuinely worsens (sNV 1.23 → 1.35), core σ +0.011. The full-recal config is also 2.7× faster (0.39 s/fit) with best-yet X implied-v flatness (0.9) — a defensible speed variant, not a quality upgrade.
  • Conclusion: Y's deficiency is kernel shape, not amplitude or speed. No recalibration of the current one-pole form can win; the real fix (a transmission-line response) is the post-MPGD26 project. lp2 + the σ = 5 prior stays the recommendation.

7.4 · Dead channels as censored samples (T1.3)

Bundles now carry a rate-based dead mask (a broken connection still shows a normal pedestal, so the mask comes from fire rates inside candidate windows). Dead rows leave the χ² sum and the dof exactly like saturated samples, with the one-sided penalty disabled — no information in either direction. det3's sample has no dead channels (438/441 judged channels healthy), so the machinery is pinned by unit test and pays off on det2 (half-dead X) and det4.

7.5 · The explanatory set for the talk (T1.4)

Three real-data figures (wft/explain/) plus doc prose (erf = area under the Gaussian between the strip's two edges; the Lawson–Hanson steps behind the NNLS solve; the profile-likelihood caveats; §9 softened to "stable enough to display, too unstable to measure from").
